The intelligence contained the deployment of the enemy forces and what was to be expected from these forces in the course of Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It is true, is it not, that on the basis of such intelligence you selected the targets to be engaged at a given moment at different stages of the operation?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For Their Honours' benefit, the document identical in contents but dating from a different period, is D1052 -- or, rather, 1092, 1093, and 1098. We're referring to military targets, of course. You said that one of the targets was communications. You just described for us the -- the importance of the Celavac radio relay feature as well as the Prezid feature. And in the course of your testimony, you said that other targets were warehouses, command posts, assembly posts, which constituted the targets your artillery engaged. Is that correct, Mr. Turkalj?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We will now discuss an artillery issue, and I presume you will be able to help us with it, in view of your relevant experience. Can you explain to us the meaning in artillery -- in the artillery sense, the firing of a projectile upon a military target in order to -- with a view to disrupting it, as opposed to firing a projectile upon a military target with a view to neutralizing. What is the different -- from a -- in terms of artillery?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Engaging a target to neutralize it would mean that great many more projectiles would need to be used, and when we're talking about command posts or communication centres, neutralizing them would mean placing them out of operation. In other words, such locations could not -- no longer be used as venues for commanding or engaging in any sort of activity. Neutralizing it means to make it impossible for these features to operate. Disrupting a target means to fire a small number of projectiles upon that location, in order to diminish its capacity to engage in the activities that location normally engages in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Judging from the tactics the artillery of the special police employed in the early stages of Operation Storm, would you say that they engaged in -- they engaged targets with a view to neutralizing them or disrupting their activity?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Well, if we're talking about the targets deep behind the front line, then the intention was to disrupt their activity; whereas the targets that were on the front line, or immediately behind the front line, then the intention was to neutralize their activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the strongholds held by the enemy which were used to fire upon the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat his answer because there was no break between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you make breaks between question and answer, and could you repeat your last answer because the interpreters could not hear it. So the last question was whether you were referring to the strongholds held by the enemy which were used to fire upon the Croatian forces. Could you repeat your answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't received interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you now receive interpretation? Apparently not. Let's check. Do you now hear me in a language you understand? Yes. You were invited to repeat the -- your answer to the last question, and the last question being whether you were referring to the strongholds held by the enemy which were used to fire upon the Croatian forces. Could you please repeat your answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer was that the targets to be neutralized were the strongholds held by the enemy, which engaged in artillery fire upon the Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once the first defence line of the enemy was broken through and in the subsequent activities that the special police engaged in, what sort of tactics did the artillery engage in?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Can I just make an introduction to this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Given the lie of the land as the Croatian forces were advancing toward the foot of the Velebit mount pretty quickly, we were not longer able to rely upon the artillery support because of the range that they had. For these purposes, we used the artillery that was attached to the special police in order to make sure that our forces could further advance, until such time as the special police artillery was able to redeploy to new positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can we make a difference now in the number of spent ammunition in relation to the first part of the action, which is Velebit, compared to the next part of the action. Which part of the action, the first or the second, used more artillery shells, depending on the phase of the action?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Depending on the phase of the action, the most artillery was spent breaking through the first line of defence. It is difficult to give you a percentage, but most of the artillery -- or more artillery was spent in that phase.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that that was a demanding hilly area, mostly uninhabited. Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, there was a question about shelling in the following phase of the action on the town of Gracac. In this courtroom, we heard testimony from an eye-witness of this shelling who lived in Gracac. I'm now referring to the testimony of Mr. Mile Sovilj. And he told us, and this is transcript page 2241, line 8, that the shelling of Gracac that day when Oluja started proceeded at intervals and that, from what he recalled, he remembers about some 15 shells following on the area of Gracac where he lived. Can you please tell us from -- based on your recollection how many shells were fired at Gracac, the town itself? Does this number correspond to what you know?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, I think that the number is accurate, about the number of projectiles fired at Gracac itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you're talking about targets, I assume that you are referring to military targets?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes. I'm exclusively talking about targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But these targets are in inhabited areas, populated areas, in civilian areas, let's put it that way. You have already explained to the Prosecution that this had to be done very precisely, in order to minimise possible collateral damage. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The same witness, Mr. Mile Sovilj, in his testimony said that in the centre of Gracac itself, there was a police station, the municipal building as well where the national or people's defence office was. There was railway station, intersection of the roads from Knin to Zagreb and towards Otric, then depot next to the railway station, which the witness -- about which the witness said that that's where he saw certain weapons. Does that correspond with your recollection of the facilities and the buildings in Gracac and the targets?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, those were the targets.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I think we have a practice here when we put previous continue testimony from other witnesses to a witness in court, there is an practice as to how that should be done. I think this is the second time Mr. Mikulicic has breached that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I was trying to save some time and not to quote all the parts of testimony of witness Mile Sovilj, and, therefore, I gave the reference. And the reference, I could repeat, starts from transcript page 2241 --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's not what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, let's be -- of course, if you ask a witness to describe a certain event, then -- then it makes sense to hear the version of the present witness and after that to perhaps put to him what another witness said about it. But to first ask him whether there was a railway station there, and then to say, Well, that's what Mr. Sovilj told us as well. Of course, it doesn't make sense. I do agree with you that is the rules, but, of course, rules should be applied always in context. And here the only thing until now is that in the centre of Gracac itself, there was the municipal building; there was a railway station; there was an intersection -- well, these intersections usually do not move very quickly, so, therefore, looking at it in the context, it is more efficient to put these simple matters to this witness. It could even have been put to him separate from Mr. Sovilj's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I only rose to my feet because the witness has already testified in examination-in-chief as to what targets were present in Gracac and also the previous question as to the number of shells fired at Gracac. The witness should have been asked that, and then thereafter if there was a contradiction to -- with the previous testimony. That is why, Mr. President, that I feel that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, whether he has testified in chief, that is, of course, a different matter. And it would even, I would say, undermine, more or less, your objection because -- if he had already testified about it, then, of course, the procedure which is to seek the testimony of the witness before putting to him what other witness said apparently has then already been met. Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I guess so, Mr. President. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's try to -- to interpret rules and guidance and context and with full understanding of what it is all about. Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Turkalj, the first lines of defence of the enemy were broken through in the first half of the day, and then you said that after that you descended down the slopes of the Velebit towards the road leading from Gospic towards Gracac. The pace of the events was quite considerable, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if the command insisted on this pace of advance of the special unit?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: The command of the special unit insisted, depending on the conditions at the front, at the time the situation on the front line, the breakthrough of the front line, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your experience, why was the pace of advance in these actions important for special units which are actually pushing back enemy forces, why is this pace important?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Well, it's now a question of tactics, but the main assignment was not to permit the enemy forces to group, and, in that way, to create a second line of defence, which would then place before us the same problem of having to breakthrough that second line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You told us that, in your view, the bulk of the artillery was spent in that first phase.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I would now like us to look at document P1154. 1154.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What we are going to see, Mr. Turkalj, is a request from the special police sent on the second day of the action, the 5th of August, to the Ministry of Defence, to General Cervenko, the chief of the Main Staff, for replenishment of ammunition for the requirements of the special police. Not going into too much detail, I would just like to you comment. We can see that what is being asked here under the first two items are 120-millimetre mines and 128-millimetre missiles or projectiles. And then later, missiles for a hand-held rocket launcher. According to the categories that we referred to earlier, short-range, medium-range and long-range artillery, what would be the purpose of these projectiles? Are these projectiles for long-range weaponry or --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: These are projectiles for short-range artillery. The other projects are anti-armour ammunition or shells which the members carry with them. And then we see also replenishment and guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And was this request implemented to the letter? Was all this weaponry and ammunition delivered to the special police units, or were there some logistical imprecisions, if we can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: The question of replenishment was something that was under the jurisdiction of the logistics section, so I don't know how much actually of this was delivered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: My question had to do with document P614, which was an analysis of Storm, and on page 35 negative experience from the action are referred to from the operation. And then in item 5, it says that untimely support in ammunition for the artillery was a negative aspect resulting in more difficulties for those firing positions, because they were supplied under enemy fire. Do you recall such problems occurring?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, there was such problems. In an operation like that, it can happen for the ammunition not to arrive in time especially in the sector where our logistical forces were moving and the artillery was shifting to new positions and then fire was opened from enemy artillery in those sections, so it was not that easy to organise everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar now please show us D1095.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I'd like to take the opportunity to ask one additional question. Where you several times refer to short-range and long-range artillery weaponry, where does the short-range move into long-range? What is approximately where you ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Targets on the first line of defence, enemy defence, and for shorter depth - we're talking about targets that would be in contact with the Croatian forces, where the two forces were in contact - that's where short-range artillery would be used, in the area of attack. Long-range artillery would be used in the course of the operations for targets in the depth, and these artilleries would be separate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you express that in distances.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All targets that are farther than eight kilometres could only be fired at with long-term -- long range artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at document D1095.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Other than this problem that was indicated as a negative experience in the analysis of the Storm operation, we can also see from this document that the weapons malfunctioned. And now I'm drawing your attention to paragraph 4, the biggest paragraph, on the first page where it says that : "The 130-millimetre gun was jammed, that the 203-millimetre Howitzer also broke down. According to this categorisation. We're talking about medium or long-range weaponry, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And does what you know correspond to what it says there, that there were malfunctions while using artillery?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at document P586, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the examination-in-chief, Mr. Turkalj, battles were discussed and the use of artillery in Donji Lapac. You are now going to see this document. It has already been admitted into evidence, and it's a report from the chief, Mr. Branislav Bole, chief of logistics, sent to the chief of sector, Mr. Zeljko Sacic. It had to do with the fighting to liberate Donji Lapac. Mr. Turkalj, first of all, it is correct, isn't it, that the special police actually did not use artillery in the fighting to liberate Donji Lapac itself?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. This is what I have already stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Then what it says here in paragraph 2 is that although there were no major battles in the town of Donji Lapac, in the town centre two houses were burning as a consequence of artillery rocket support actions. But then later major incidents occurred in town, and houses were set on fire. Were you an eye-witness of these events, Mr. Turkalj?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: From what I know -- I was also in Donji Lapac myself when forces of the special police entered that sector. In any case, because of my duties, I was among the last to arrive. Could you please repeat the question about what I know. Are you asking about what I know about how Donji Lapac looked?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: As for Donji Lapac itself, it wasn't burned or destroyed. There was no destruction, and I would even say that everything appeared quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has already heard testimony that there was a friendly fire incident in Donji Lapac. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How long did this friendly fire at special police forces last before radio communication was established, asking for the artillery firing to stop?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: It was difficult -- it's difficult to say how long it lasted, if fire in the area. Perhaps it's not quite correct to say on Donji Lapac but somewhere in that area at the entrances to Donji Lapac, or whatever the targets were that the artillery was firing, but it did last for minutes, perhaps even several scores of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at document 06171, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I assume, Mr. Turkalj, that you didn't have the opportunity to see this document, because this is a document on the participation of the rocket and artillery battery of the Brod-Posavina unit in the Operation Storm Oluja 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I haven't seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm going ask for your comments on the document then. Based on the description of the equipment and materiel in the second paragraph of the document, can you please tell us what sort of artillery is talking -- being talked about here?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: It is artillery that the special police had, and we can see here that it includes only 120-millimetre mortars and RAK 12, which is a 128-millimetre rocket launcher. The rest had nothing to do with artillery but with vehicles. As for the rocket Strijela 2M, it has to do with anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was this artillery, as part of the Brod-Posavina police administration special forces, which through its engagement with the joint forces of the special police forces, made its pieces available for use to the joint forces? Was this the method applied in order to establish the joint forces?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes. It was that method, and the same principle was used with other units and their artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the last paragraph on this page, I would like to elicit a comment from you. It says: "It was also agreed on a who can ask for artillery support." Can you comment on this sentence of the report?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The commander of the battery, who I suppose forwarded this report, was at the meeting prior to the operation and familiarized with the principles to ask for artillery support and what was the axis of attack that he was supposed to engage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If we go to page 2 of this document, please focus on paragraph 2, which says that, on the 4th of August of 1995 upon the beginning of the operation at 0400 hours, he explained to the members, and "he" is probably the submitter of the report, Mr. Andrija Zivkovic, commander of the rocket artillery battery, how we would perform the rocket artillery operations on the targets already designated. "At 0520 hours we fired the first rockets and shells and the artillery support lasted for about half an hour." Now we come to the part that I'm interested in: "And then we only opened fire pursuant to a request of Mr. Josip Turkalj who was chief of artillery of the special units." This was then the procedure applied when the artillery forces of the joint forces were used?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, that was the procedure. The commanders could ask me to engage certain targets, and I would approve of such targeting at the artillery position. It wasn't only up to me to designate targets. The axis commanders could also request fire support. However this position was relatively close to me, and I could supervise their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I receive a number for this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1206, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1206 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 05612 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Perhaps later we are going to discuss the establishment of the joint forces of the police that participated in Operation Storm. This Chamber has already heard evidence of the joint forces being formed in a way that from individual police administrations, parts of special police forces units were joined and that a common headquarters was established that was in charge of the operation. What we can see on the screen is an order of the 27th of July, that is on the eve of Operation Storm, issued by assistant minister, Mr. Mladen Markac, sent to the chiefs of four police administrations personally, as well as to you, as the ATJ unit, Lucko commander. As we can see from the order, it discusses the gathering of artillery pieces from the units of the special police. It is stated that from the Osijek-Baranja police administration, two 120-millimetre mortars should be attached to the joint forces, and the same goes for the Sisak-Moslavina police administration. As for the Karlovac police administration, what was requested was a four-member crew, and from the police administration of Zagreb, an additional two mortars were requested. Mr. Turkalj, in relation to what we have discussed so far, this is the operational implementation of the manning of the joint forces of the police with artillery pieces.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, this was sent to the chiefs of police administrations, and they were supposed to hand this order to the commanders of their respective special forces. It is also stipulated here where those commanders were supposed to report to, so as to be issued with specific artillery tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Therefore, that was the model used to establish the artillery of the joint forces for operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please receive a number for this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1270.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1207 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Turkalj, as for you and the members of the special police that serviced the artillery pieces, did you have or did you receive proper training on the use of artillery in keeping with the Geneva Conventions and related protocols?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes. The commanders of the batteries that we have been discussing of the special police received orders from me providing instruction on the use of artillery, and they also conducted training with their respective staff on the use of artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Briefly, in two sentences, could you tell us what was the essence of the instructions you issued on the use of artillery in keeping with the laws of war?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: The essence was that only military targets could be engaged, and we did so in that part of the attack operation. Tactically speaking, it also addressed the issue of artillery, in the sense of how to neutralize enemy targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. In the analysis document of the special police, which is P614, Mr. Turkalj, concerning the use of artillery at page 23 that we have already seen, it is stated, I will quote: "Through their efficient use, meaning the artillery, the fortified enemy positions and facilities were destroyed as well as the strategic military targets in depth of the enemy were engaged, thus creating psychological uncertainty and anxiety among the ranks of the enemy as well as the Serbian population?" Mr. Turkalj, in your experience and education during the Military Academy, it is correct, is it not, that the use of artillery carries a relatively significant psychological effect. Can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Artillery does have a psychological impact in order to demoralize enemy forces. It is one of its basic tasks to demoralize the enemy. As for the use of artillery against military targets, irrespective of whether it is in proximity or distance from settlements does have a certain psychological effect on the population in the area as well. This last sentence is basically a statement of mine, a comment of mine. Artillery as such can cause fear among the population as well as the forces in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the effect of explosions and detonations upon firing. You also said that it was a mountainous terrain with gorges and valleys. In your opinion, and expertise, what is the effect of detonations and firing of shells from artillery pieces in such terrain?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: As for the lie of land, perhaps there is a part I would like to add to your question an offer a single reply. When we destroyed the communications centre of the enemy as well as our targeting of the radio relay facility enabled -- did not enable them to communicate effectively anymore, and engaging other targets along the axis of attack of the special forces did have a certain negative impact on the persons in the vicinity. Such persons can not precisely determine where detonations came from; they only hear them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. However, I'd just like to go back to one part of your answer because it wasn't recorded. What was your personal view on the use of artillery? You said that the population could suffer feelings of fear, of anxiety?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I said that I would also be scared if I heard artillery being active nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you this: In a mountainous terrain with depressions and gorges, there's an echo effect amplifying the noises of firing, multiplying them, so to speak. Is that a byproduct, so to speak, of the use of artillery?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes. I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Therefore, it is correct that a layperson, when artillery is used in such geographical conditions could conclude that there was a far greater number of shells that were fired, given the echo effect than the number that was actually fired?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: One could conclude that. In such geographical conditions it is very difficult to assess how many projectiles were fired at individual targets if a person concerned has no particular knowledge and experience with artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As regards, artillery, Your Honours, this concludes there topic, unless you have questions about that, otherwise I will move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Turkalj, we are going to discuss the topic of the joint forces of the special police next. We saw, and you mentioned that as well, that Mr. Markac, the assistant minister, who was actually the commander of the special police sector, he sent an order to certain police administration commanders as regards personnel, materiel, and equipment. In your experience and, knowledge, what was the relationship between the special police unit commander at the police administration vis-a-vis the head of that police administration?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Well, I would try to it turn your question around a bit. The special unit of the police was a part of the police administration structure. It was part and parcel of it. The head of that police administration was responsible for the work of that particular special police unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am not going to talk to -- about the joint forces now but, rather, on the use of the special police forces. Could a police administration head independently decide on the use of the special police unit inside his police administration, within its territory?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: As regards the tasks of the special police, the head of the police administration would exclusively decide on the orders and decisions concerning daily use and work of that particular special unit in that area. It was the head of the police administration who could issue orders to the unit, and he was in charge of the use of that unit in his area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In situations such as Operation Storm, when joint forces are formed, joint forces of the police that is, from individual police administrations, including all of them save for the ones that did not have special police units, some members of the special police units' staff were assigned to the joint forces. Those of the staff who remained in their respective police administrations, what was their role and who decided on the tasks of those special police who remained within their respective administrations?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Those members of the special police units who did not participate in the joint forces remained under the competence of the head of the police administration, and he issued them tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you well, it means that the headquarters of the joint forces, vis-a-vis those special police forces that did not participate in the joint forces held no sway?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: However, if the head the police administration should, for whatever reasons, and I'm not even referring to combat here or the mop-up operation, but, for instance, civil unrest taking place in the territory outside of the purview of that particular police administration, should therefore the police of that particular police administration have to be engaged outside of its purview of competence, then it has to apply to the minister; does it not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes. It has to apply to the Ministry of the Interior to allow it to use its staff outside of their respective police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The unit you were the head of, the anti-terrorist unit Lucko, was of a specific sort because it did not fall under any of the police administrations. Rather, it was a part of the sector of the special police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, because that particular unit was present in the Ministry of Interior before other special police units were formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your unit, and I don't mean this disrespectfully toward anyone, had the status of an elite unit within the Ministry of Interior compared to the other special police units belonging to various administrations.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, you could say that it enjoyed the status of an elite unit, although in combat activities, it was not given any specific role for that score only, nevertheless, it did enjoy a special status.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: There are -- there is statistical data speaking of the dead and injured members of the anti-terrorist unit Lucko, as opposed to other members of the special police forces in that particular operation. And it is true, is it not, that it was precisely your anti-terrorist unit Lucko which suffered a great number of dead and injured?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: That's true. From day one of the war in Croatia, it was engaged in almost all important war activities and had more dead and wounded than any other unit in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, let me go back to the events which transpired on the 25th and 26th of August, 1995. Let me remind you that the so-called freedom train was supposed to travel the railway between Zagreb and Split. Do you remember that period?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It is true, is it not, that to that end, the anti-terrorist unit Lucko was engaged in the most sensitive section of the railway, where the train was supposed to travel, holding the president of the republic, ministers, and many of the diplomates accredited in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Once the freedom train passed the railway track from Zagreb and reached Split, the anti-terrorist unit Lucko was dispatched back to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: That's correct. I said that in my statement that Mr. Janjic as commander of the action did not deem its presence necessary there anymore and ordered that it return to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did rumour reach you to the effect that once the freedom train finished its journey, the return of the anti-terrorist unit Lucko to Zagreb was some sort of a punishment for the crimes that were committed in one of the villages?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, the commander believed that the unit needs to go back to its base, since its task was finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it true, is it not, Mr. Turkalj, that the operational action of providing security to the railway track to be travelled by the freedom train ended as the train reached Split?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have document D1084, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... there was an observation by the interpreters that the interpreters could not hear the name of the villages, if you would please look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The name of the village is Ramljane. R-a-m-l-j-a-n-e.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Turkalj, the former Minister of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Vekic, issued this document at the end of 1991. My first question is: Have you seen this order before, ever before?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I have never seen this order. At least I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you to comment certain portions of the document. In practice, in the everyday life and work, did the anti-terrorist unit conduct itself in line with this particular order? And I'm referring to items 5 and the subsequent items. It says here that for every special unit formed, its reserve force has to be set up as well, equal in number to the active duty unit. Is this consistent with the practice you came to know while you worked with the special police?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, in principle it does tally with how it worked in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who were members of the reserve force of the special police unit?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Members of reserve force units in the various police administrations were citizens who were charged with certain duties in the police. Both the general duty police and the special police force had its reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Am I right in interpreting your answer by saying these were individuals with police training?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, they did have some sort of police training through their work. As the reserve force, they underwent police staining.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is particularly what item 6 speaks to, namely that the reserve forces of the special unit would be formed of members of the reserve force of the special police according to the criteria set in place for active-duty special policemen. Item 7 reads: "The special units are to be engaged solely pursuant to decisions issued by the chief of police administration and deputy minister of the interior or the person thus authorised by him." It seems that what you've just said confirms the practice, as it was?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we turn to page 2 of the document to look at item 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where the minister orders that the -- that before engaging a special unit in the area of his administration, the chief of a police administration must obtain clearance from the deputy minister or the person authorised by the him. It seems to me, and you will correct me if I'm wrong, that the practice is somewhat modified this decision, and that the chief of a police administration subsequently did not need to obtain the approval from the minister or the deputy minister to use his forces within the territory of the administration but only when it came to their use outside of the police administration.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, for the territory of an administration -- of a police administration, it was solely the chief of that particular police administration that would approve the use of the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But if we look at item 9, it speaks of this other situation, where the police is being used in the territory of a different police administration, where it cannot be used, meaning the police force, without the approval from the deputy minister. This is consistent with your experience, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, when the combat activities of the joint forces of the special police were over, there remained another task which was, according to the order of the chief of the Main Staff within the purview of the joint forces, and that was the duty of the -- the duty to carry out search and mop-up operations outside the inhabited areas. This was something that was carried out by the special police; was it not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: To your recollection, and based on your experience, can you tell us what the main task was in the search operation that was assigned to the special police?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: As far as I remember, since the HV and special police units advanced very quickly in Operation Storm, which meant that certain groups of enemy soldiers could have found themselves cut off and lingered in mountainous areas, that are difficult to control, the special police was given the order to conduct a search operation in order to detect, sabotage terrorist groups or groups of enemy soldiers who stayed behind after their forces were routed in Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We spoke of the pace at which our units, meaning the military and the special police forces advanced during Operation Storm. Is it true, is it not, that the advancements was made along certain roads and axes and some of the terrain not covered by these, i.e., the mountainous area, stayed behind, was not cleared up or certain pockets were formed where one could not be sure whether there were any mines laid or lingering stragglers of enemy forces, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's what I said. There were certain areas not covered in the initial stages of Storm and were left behind, and there were -- there was materiel and technical equipment, explosives, and weapons that had been wielded by the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Before we make the break, the area that was searched by the special police in this search and mop-up operation was difficult to access; was it not? Did you ever have occasion to hear or see that the special police force had conducted such search operations in inhabited areas, villages or towns?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: As far as I know, the special police conducted such operations solely in the elevated feature, such as the Petrova Gora or the Plitvice lakes which is a forested area, difficult to survey. The areas of [indiscernible] and similar features.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, it's time for a break. May I remind you, and also you, Mr. Turkalj, that the speed which you develop in question and answer gives the interpreters a hard time today, so if could you please slow down and make these breaks. So we will have a break, and we will resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Turkalj, before we had the break, we were discussing joint forces and search operations. First let me put a question to you about the setting up of the joint forces. The joint forces of the special police could also be set up for the purposes of combat activities but also for purely regular policing tasks, such as policing rioting, any other sort of unrest, and so on and so forth; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Registrar please call up D1089.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The document we're about to see dates from August 1992, and is, in fact, a proposal from the then-chief of the special police department, Mr. Markac, which was sent to assistant minister Josko Moric. Later on when we look at page 2, we will see that assistant minister Josko Moric approved the proposal, as did deputy minister Zeljko Tomljenovic. This is a proposal for establishing action Poskok, horned viper, in the area of Velebit. You are familiar with Poskok action that the special police conducted in the area of Mount Velebit?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it true, is it not, that the idea behind the whole action was to prevent the breakthrough from the enemy forces across the Velebit mount, and out on to the -- from preventing it from coming out on the seaward side, and thus cutting off Croatia into two parts, northern and southern parts; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In this document General Markac, in fact, proposes the tasks of the special police within the action as a whole. Please look at item 3, locating sabotage terrorist groups, their capturing, disarmament, bringing in, and destroying. Item 4, locating, identifying, marking and, in cooperation with the Croatian army engineering team, demounting and destroying mine-explosive devices. On the next page, items 5 and 6, speak about the fact that the special police, as part of its work, has to engage in detecting all manner of explosive devices hidden away in various caches and hideouts on the Velebit mount, as well as detecting dead bodies, and burials, graves. In fact, these were the tasks discharged by the special police as it was conducting searches and mopping up areas; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes. These are identical tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The tasks were defined in light of the fact that the members of the special police had specialist knowledge. Primarily I'm referring to scuba divers, speleology, explosive specialists, and so on and so forth. It is true, is it not, that members of the special police had to go through specialist training and specialize in various fields?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Every unit had organised, specialized groups, the ones that you referred to, and they had to go through their regular training alongside their regular work. And it had to do with the specialist knowledge you to referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Based on the specialist knowledge and training members of the special police under went, they were used for special purpose missions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, I will be changing topics now. I am not doing this in the proper order, but this is because I omitted to next something, and I have to get back to it now. You remember when we discussed the use of artillery, I showed you the order from the chief of the Main Staff to engage special police units in Operation Storm. This order is now marked as D1205. This order was sent to Brigadier Ademi for his information. You will remember that Brigadier Rajko Rakic added in his hand an observation that the area had to be reinforced with artillery. I would now like to you look at D1094. When Brigadier Rakic placed his remark on the order sent for their information about the reinforced artillery - this was on the 29th of July, 1995 - the chief of the Main Staff, General Cervenko, reacted with a 30th July order --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This isn't the document. Can we have D1049. That's 65 ter 2162.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: There seems as if we have small technical problems, but perhaps we can do it without this document. Here it is. Can we look at item 4. In this order by General Cervenko, which followed the next day after the remark by Brigadier Rakic about the use of artillery, General Cervenko orders that forces engaged on the slopes of Velebit to be provided with a special artillery group that would provide them - referring to the HVO forces - and the MUP forces with artillery support. One question about this, Mr. Turkalj. It's correct, isn't it, that only the chief of the Main Staff was authorised to order artillery support and then that order was operationally implemented at the level of army command?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes. It would be further operationally implemented in the Military Districts that it applied to, relating to artillery support.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, I'm at the end of my cross-examination, and I would just like to put a few more questions to you. We talked about how, on the 25th of August, or, rather, the 26th of August, an incident took place in the village of Grubori and in the area of the village of Ramljane where some houses were set on fire, and some persons were killed in the village of Grubori. And we talked in that sense that there were a lot of contested facts, and you tried to explain that, as well as some other witnesses who were here. In relation to that, this is my question, did you ever, or anyone that you know, received from the superior structures within the police or the state government in general, any kind of instruction, oral or written, that these events should be covered up, that they should not be investigated, that they should -- or that the facts relating to those incidents in Grubori should be concealed? Did you know anything like that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to try to respond very simply to your question. I don't know. I did not, nor did I hear of any other of my colleagues received any kind of instruction to cover up any event that happened over those few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, thank you very much for your answers. I'm going conclude my with that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Who is next in line, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, you will you now be cross-examined by Mr. Kay. Mr. Kay is counsel for Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, where were you when you first heard that an incident had happened in the Plavno valley in Grubori on the 25th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't get a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question. Where were you when you first heard -- I'll start again because we may have switched channels. I don't know. Where were you when you first heard that on the 25th of August, in Grubori, in the Plavno valley, that there had been an incident and people were killed?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: As you already know from my statement, I said that I was not in the area during those few days, and I think that it was only on the 27th that I was called to that area, and that was the first time that I received information about an incident or event happening in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So on the 25th of August, where were you on that day?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: On the 25th of August, I was working in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you didn't hear anything about an incident in Grubori whilst you were in Zagreb, on that day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: That is right. I didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On the next day, the 26th of August, were you still in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you hear anything on that day about an incident happening in Grubori, in the Plavno valley?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So moving, then, to the 27th, what time of day was it that you heard that something had happened on the 25th?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the exact time, but it was sometime in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And where exactly were you when you heard that information in the morning?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I was in the area of Plavno and of Grubori.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And why had you gone to Grubori in the area of Plavno on the 27th? What caused you to go there on that day?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I have already said in my testimony that I was called by Mr. Sacic to come to Plavno because there was certain activities there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On the 27th, then, when Mr. Sacic called you, where were you when you received that call?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I was in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in what particular place?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I could have been at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And so how did he communicate to you whilst you were in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: By telephone, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And so you left Zagreb, and you went where from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I went to the Gracac area and then continued towards Plavno.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, in Gracac, where exactly did you go?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I only met Mr. Celic and Mr. Balunovic in Gracac. I didn't go anywhere specifically; we just with met up in Gracac and then continued on our way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you travel from Zagreb to Gracac on your own?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what place did you meet Mr. Celic and Mr. Balunovic at in Gracac?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where we met. We met somewhere in Gracac itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, was it on the street, in a cafe, or in an office?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: We met in front of the building where the staff of the special police was. But I cannot definitely say where it was. But I think that's where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Had you ever been to that building in Gracac before the 27th of August?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And just thinking about the time again, as we've got there in front of the special police building, are you able to think again and recollect what time of day that you met Mr. Celic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: We met sometime in the morning. Maybe around 7.00 or 8.00, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you meet Mr. Sacic when you were in Gracac?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I don't remember. No, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you speak to Mr. Sacic when you were in Gracac?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I did not meet Mr. Sacic when I was in Gracac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How long did you spend in Gracac, having met Mr. Celic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: We didn't stay long in Gracac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So from Gracac, where did you then go?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: After Gracac, we went to the area of Plavno.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And how long did it take you to get from Gracac to this area of Plavno?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: It's hard to say, but perhaps about an hour and a half, two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And when you say "in the area of Plavno," is that the village of Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: No. I'm thinking about the area of the settlement of Plavno itself. It's a bit below the village of Grubori.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And thinking again, what time of day would that have been, if you're able to tell us, when you arrived in Plavno village?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: It's hard to say exactly what time it was. Perhaps it was around 10.00. It's hard to be specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you travel from Gracac to Plavno on your own or with anybody?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I travelled alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Celic and Mr. Balunovic also go to Plavno at the same time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes. But they had another vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Celic tell you why you were going to Plavno?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Mr. Celic didn't tell me that. I've already said that Mr. Sacic told me that I was to go to the village of Plavno because there was a specific event that happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, taking this in stages, did Mr. Sacic describe to you what the specific event was, what had happened?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: No, he didn't describe anything specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So what did he describe then, if he didn't describe anything specifically? What did he say to you was your mission and reason for going to Plavno?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: He didn't mention any specific assignment. No such assignment was given to me. He just called and said that I was supposed to go to that area, and this is what I did. The alleged reason was that there had been some event in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, looking at it, then, why did you go to Gracac first and not drive direct to Plavno?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: For the simple reason that I didn't know where the settlement or the village of Plavno was. I'd never been in that area before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So when you went to Gracac, was Mr. Celic expecting you to come to Gracac?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I told Mr. Celic to come to Gracac so then we can go -- we could go to the area of Plavno, because I didn't know that area of Plavno at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Had anyone else told Mr. Celic that he should go to Plavno, or was it just as a result of your request?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was as a result of my request that we should meet in Gracac and then continue on to Plavno, because I didn't know where Plavno was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So had you telephoned him in advance to say that you were coming down?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: No. He also set off from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did he travel down with you from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: No. Everyone had their own vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you travel together, although in separate vehicles?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know that he was travelling from Zagreb at the same time as you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes. I told him to go to the Gracac area so that, later, we could go to the Plavno area together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Balunovic, did he travel down from Zagreb as well?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: He went together with Mr. Celic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Who arrived in Gracac first? You or Mr. Celic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Mr. Celic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So he was waiting for you there, was he?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, we met in front of the building. Perhaps he arrived five or ten minutes before I did, but I'm not able to say exactly how much earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Celic explain to you why you were going to Plavno?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: No. I called Mr. Celic to come with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Looking at that in two parts, then, when you called Mr. Celic, did he say anything to you about what had happened in Plavno?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: No. I've already said that I didn't speak with Mr. Celic before that. Only when we arrived at Plavno.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But when you met Mr. Celic in Gracac outside the special police building, did you have a conversation with him as to why you were going to the Plavno area?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: No. We didn't discuss those questions specifically. I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So he didn't make any explanation to you on that morning of the 27th of August as to why you needed to go to Plavno?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: No, not that time. I said that when we came to Plavno, we were together, and that was when we talked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just one matter of detail. Did you travel that morning before you went to Grubori to Knin? Before you went to Grubori.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Where did you stop in the village of Plavno with Mr. Celic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly. I'm not really that familiar with that area. That was the first time that I was there, and I never went back there again. But we stopped somewhere close to Grubori, somewhere on the road. I don't know the name of that place. I'm -- I can't say that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And how long did you stop there for?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I'm not able to say that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have a discussion with Mr. Celic before you later went to Grubori as to what had happened in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I mentioned in my statement what we talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I want you to answer my question, though. You may have said many things in your statement, but I want you to answer my questions. I'll repeat it. Did you have a discussion with Mr. Celic before you later went to Grubori as to what had happened in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact details of the conversation, but we talked about the assignments of the unit, we talked, he explained the area, more or less where the unit was supposed to sweep the terrain. He explained to me, and I said this in my statement, that he wrote this statement and that after the statement, while he was talking with Mr. Sacic, he wrote an additional report about the circumstances. He also told me that he was not at that place, since there was some other assignments he was executing at that time. Specifically, he was somewhere else. And he doesn't know what happened in that area. That was more or less the gist of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. So before you went to Grubori, did you know that there had been an assertion that there had been a fight between the special police units and terrorists in that area?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: The only information that I had, and that was that precise information, is that there had been a fight there with the opposing forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. You then went to Grubori. And how many houses in that village were you able to see?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: We didn't search the houses. When a number of the people who were in Grubori, when they came to that area, we saw that whole area more or less, but I had the feeling that you could see perhaps in two or three houses that there had been possible fighting. There were traces of weapons, of bullets, traces on the walls of the houses. The houses were not burned or showed other kind of damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you speak to Mr. Sacic whilst you were in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: No, I didn't speak to Mr. Sacic about anything in particular. I've already said that there were several people there, and Mr. Sacic and I did not talk with one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Sacic spoke to Mr. Celic whilst you were in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I don't recall him talking with Mr. Celic then, when he was in Grubori.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Whilst you were in Grubori, did a group of people also enter the village which were journalists, General Cermak, and other people, amounting to about 30 people?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I cannot say how many people were there when the group came to that area, but there were many people. That's why it's hard to say who talked with whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of you being actually there physically in Grubori at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: You mean me personally or the group?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You personally.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I was not under the impression that my presence there was required or important for anything. However, it is a fact that Mr. Sacic called me and told me that I was supposed to go to that area. Other than that, I had no specific tasks there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you present in Grubori when there were any discussions about there having been a combat at that -- on the 25th of August between the special police and the terrorist forces?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I was present in the settlement of Grubori as a member of the group you referred to. There were no specific discussions that took place. However, there were several people there, and they were talking to each other. Therefore, I suppose that they did exchange comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you hear such comments being made that the special police had been involved in a combat action with Serbian terrorist forces?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, there were such remarks made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Where you were and what you saw, did it look like, to you, that that could have been an explanation as to what had happened in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: As I have said already, as far as I could assess, the looks of the area, I concluded that there was fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You're a member of the special police. Are you able to name the other types of people, if there were any, other than special police who were in Grubori during your visit?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: While I was in Grubori, I know that Mr. Celic and Mr. Balunovic were there who arrived with me. There was Mr. Sacic. There was some other members of the HV. There was some civilians. I can't say specifically who was there in the settlement of Grubori.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know if there were or were not members of the ordinary civilian police also there at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I think there were representatives of the civilian police. However, I do not remember who they were or what their names were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How long did you spend in Grubori during this visit?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: It was a relatively short period of time, 15 to 20 minutes. I can't be any more precise than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: From Grubori, you then went where? Where was the next place you went to?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: From Grubori, we went downhill to the area of Plavno, where we stayed for a relatively short time as a group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And then where did you go next after that place?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: After that, we went to Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And who did you travel with?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I was in my own vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Had you ever been to Knin before?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: No, I had not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you went to Knin, what place did you go to?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I think I went to the building or facility where the Croatian army was. I don't know what the name of the building was, though. It may have been a headquarters or simply a building with the HV.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you think back now as to what time of day it was when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: It was sometime before lunch, perhaps around noon. I can't tell you the precise time, but around noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is this the time and the place where you had a cup of coffee?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, we did have a cup of coffee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And was there general discussion amongst people at that time and at that place about what had happened in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: At that place where the group was, in the room, there was discussion about general things, life and work in Knin, and its environs. There was mention made of Grubori, that it all looked like there had been fighting, but there was also some general discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that a statement that was made by Mr. Sacic at that time, that there had been a combat between the special police and a Serbian terrorist group?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I think Mr. Sacic did mention that, that he did mention that while we were having coffee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have one last question on this point, Your Honour, to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was there any suggestion made by Mr. Sacic that what had happened in Grubori must be misrepresented, or a false story promoted, or people misled about what had happened?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question, because I did not understand it fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will continue my questioning tomorrow with the court's leave because I have a few other matters, and I do notice the time of the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Turkalj, I give you the same instruction as I did before, that is, that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony, whether already given or still to be given, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, 9.00. We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, the 16th of December, 9.00 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 16th day of December, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 25
